attempts.raw_response: Many individuals simply do not realize they qualify as carers, viewing their daily support as a natural extension of family duty rather than a formal role requiring assistance. This lack of self-identification creates a significant barrier to accessing vital resources and respite care. Consequently, proactive outreach strategies are essential to bridge this gap. Without targeted efforts to engage these hidden populations, the potential benefits of the dedicated worker scheme remain largely unrealized for those who need it most. Improving awareness and simplifying the identification process could help ensure that more of the estimated sixteen thousand residents receive the comprehensive support they deserve, transforming an underutilized system into a truly effective safety net for vulnerable families across the region.

pair.human_continuation: "There's an awful lot of people who are caring for people and don't realise that they are, and that's our biggest stumbling block," she said. "On many occasions I've been speaking to carers and they've said, 'no, no, you've got it wrong I'm not a carer, she's my mum', and they really see it as something they should do and really do not associate themselves with the name carer." Carer Val Henfield, who looks after her partner full-time, said: "The surgery keeps in regular contact with me; I now know all about the help the Carers' Centre can give me - it's really good to know they are there for me."
pair.prefix: Although carers are believed to make up 10% of the population, nowhere near this figure is known to social services. Bath and North East Somerset has over 16,000 carers. Since the scheme was introduced in 2010, 16 GP practices out of 38 now have one dedicated worker. Stumbling block Jackie Short, of Carers' Centre Bath and North East Somerset, said it was hard to identify those who needed help.

source_document.title: Half of Bath GP surgeries take up carer scheme
